checkpoints: The essence isn't "call SDKs fast" but decoupling intake from delivery.
Sending synchronously makes the API wait on the slowest provider.
Sending synchronously couples the request's success to every provider — one failure fails the whole request.
Sending synchronously lets a spike hang many requests at once, causing cascade.
A durable queue lets the producer just enqueue and return immediately, keeping latency stable.
With a queue, a spike merely lengthens the queue instead of hanging requests.
The worker consumes asynchronously and scales out on its own (Competing Consumers).
The cost of that decoupling: the HTTP response now means "accepted", not "delivered" — delivery success is confirmed later, via the worker.
A token bucket holds up to `capacity` tokens; each send consumes one, and tokens refill at `refill` per `windowMs`.
This permits a controlled burst — up to capacity instantly — then smooths to the refill rate, a behavior a plain per-second counter can't give.
A hard reset counter either lets a full-speed spike through or clamps everyone to the same trickle, with no burst headroom.
The state must sit in Redis, not process RAM, so that all producer instances share one counter (correct when scaled out) and survive restarts.
A counter kept per-instance means n instances effectively give n times the intended limit, and a restart wipes it clean.
Read-refill-decrement-write must run atomically in a single Lua script, otherwise two concurrent requests race and overshoot.
Keying `rl:<user>:<channel>` isolates each channel's quota per user.

A queue configured with unbounded (or near-infinite) `attempts` and no `removeOnFail` handling has no mechanism to stop retrying a job that always fails — a malformed payload that makes the processor throw on every attempt just keeps looping instead of ever landing in a failed/dead-letter set.

When a worker's concurrency is effectively pinned to one job at a time, a single poison job stuck in an endless retry loop permanently occupies that worker slot, starving every legitimate job queued behind it — this is exactly the symptom of one worker pinned at "processing" the same job for hours at 100% CPU.

Accepting `@Body() body: any` in the controller and mapping `channels` directly into queued jobs with no DTO or `ValidationPipe` means invalid input — an unrecognized channel, an empty message — is never rejected at the boundary; it reaches Redis and becomes the root cause of the processor throwing repeatedly downstream.

Validating at the producer boundary — a DTO with `@IsEnum` on `channels` and `@IsNotEmpty()` on `message`, wrapped in `ValidationPipe({ whitelist: true })` — rejects a bad request with HTTP 400 before it is ever enqueued, which is a distinct and complementary fix from bounding retries on the worker side.

Replacing an unbounded `attempts` setting with a realistic finite number plus exponential backoff, and enabling `removeOnFail`, gives an exhausted job a defined stopping point: it lands in the failed set for inspection instead of cycling forever between retry and processing.

In a PR review, worker starvation from an unbounded retry loop and the missing dead-letter escape are blockers because they can cause an outage, while something like a hardcoded port or a magic-number limit is a nitpick that does not change runtime behavior under failure.

Treating an unbounded retry setting as an obvious bug rather than checking intent risks decreeing over a possibly deliberate choice — someone may have wanted infinite retries for genuinely transient failures — so asking whether the behavior was intentional is part of a thorough review.

The fix is verifiable concretely: a request with an invalid channel should return HTTP 400 and never reach `addBulk`/Redis, and a payload that always fails processing should exhaust its attempts and increase the failed-set count by exactly one instead of ever returning to the active or waiting state.

A `findOne` followed by a separate `insert` costs two network round-trips to the relational database for every single message, and since this dedup check runs on every send, it puts the database on the hot path for the system's highest-frequency operation.

`findOne` and `insert` are two independent commands rather than one atomic operation, so there is a check-then-act (TOCTOU) window between them: two workers can each run `findOne`, each see no existing row, and both proceed to `insert` and call `send`, producing a duplicate delivery even though the code appears to guard against it.

A unique constraint on `messageId` only converts the race into a database error on the second `insert` after the fact — it does not stop the second worker from having already called `send()` before that insert fails, so it detects the duplicate rather than preventing it.

The fix is to stop treating deduplication as a database read-then-write and instead perform it as a single atomic Redis command, `SET dedup:{messageId} 1 NX EX <ttl>`: because the existence-check and the write happen inside one atomic operation, there is no window in which two concurrent workers can both observe the key as absent.

The `NX` flag makes the `SET` succeed only if the key does not already exist, so the command itself returns success (`"OK"`) to exactly one caller when multiple workers race on the same `messageId`, and every other caller receives `null` and skips sending.

This is a single round-trip and an O(1) key lookup, compared to the original approach's two round-trips against an indexed table, which is what removes the database from the per-message hot path at peak throughput.

The `EX` option attaches a self-expiring TTL to the dedup key, so the dedup store does not grow without bound the way a permanent `sent_messages` table would, since old entries fall out of Redis automatically once the TTL elapses.

Correctness of the fix should be verified by firing the same `messageId` concurrently from multiple workers and asserting that exactly one of them acquires the key and sends, and by comparing round-trip count and latency under load against the original SELECT-then-INSERT path to confirm the throughput improvement.

Keying the rate-limit bucket strictly per user×channel (`rl:<recipient>:<channel>`) correctly isolates one recipient's limit from another's, but Redis Cluster maps that single literal key to exactly one hash slot on exactly one shard.

When one recipient goes viral or one channel gets hammered, every request for that pair funnels through the same key, so its EVAL calls saturate one shard while every other shard in the cluster sits idle — the bottleneck is single-key contention, not total Redis capacity.

The fix is to shard the hot key into N sub-buckets (`rl:<recipient>:<channel>:<shard>` for shard in 0..N-1), each sized to `bucketCapacity/N` and `refillAmount/N`, and route each incoming request to one sub-bucket (round-robin, or hashing a request-local id mod N).
Running the same Lua script against just the routed sub-bucket keeps the per-request check O(1) and local, with no cross-shard read needed to decide allow or deny.

Because the N sub-bucket keys naturally land on different hash slots, a viral recipient's load spreads across up to N shards instead of pinning one; when the total remaining is needed (an admin dashboard, a debug endpoint), it is computed by summing the token count across all N sub-buckets.

Splitting one shared bucket into N even slices is a real trade-off, not a free win: a burst that would have fit under the single bucket can now be rejected if it lands unevenly across sub-buckets, trading some burst-smoothing accuracy for horizontal spread across shards.

For genuinely extreme keys — traffic blowing past every sub-bucket instantly — a cheap in-memory approximate counter at the edge can reject obviously-over-limit requests before they ever issue a Redis EVAL, so Redis only sees traffic with a real chance of being allowed.
Moving the rate-limit Redis onto its own instance, separate from the queue Redis used for job dequeue, prevents a hot rate-limit shard from also starving unrelated queue traffic.

The sharding change should be validated with a load test that drives one hot key alone, measuring per-key p99 latency before and after sharding, and confirming the summed aggregate across the N sub-buckets still enforces the original limit.
Define one interface — `ChannelProvider.send({recipient, message, attempt})` → `providerMessageId`, throwing a typed delivery error on failure.
That interface is implemented identically by mocks and real providers (SendGrid, SES, Twilio), each reading its own keys internally.
Model failover as an ordered chain per channel: channel → `[primary, fallback, ...]`.
The dispatcher iterates the chain in-attempt, returns on the first success (tagging the tier), and only lets the error escape when every provider in the chain fails.

Adding a provider or a third fallback only requires implementing the interface and registering it in the chain — the dispatcher and worker are never touched, and that invariance (open/closed) is exactly what makes the boundary hold.

Numeric priority inside a single queue is non-preemptive: under concurrency an OTP can still wait for a slot already busy serving marketing taken earlier, because priority only decides which waiting job is picked next, not seizing an already-running slot.

For a hard latency guarantee you must split the topology: intake classifies and routes urgent traffic (OTP/transactional) to a dedicated queue with its own reserved worker pool, and bulk traffic (marketing) to a separate queue/pool, so urgent capacity is never consumed by bulk since the lanes no longer contend for the same workers.

Keeping one shared priority queue with a bigger worker pool does not remove the risk: with enough marketing volume and high enough concurrency, most slots can already be busy on marketing jobs exactly when an OTP shows up.

Splitting lanes costs roughly double the operational overhead: two queues and two worker pools each need their own sizing and monitoring, plus an explicit routing contract defining what marks a message "urgent" so intake routes correctly and nothing mislabels into the urgent lane.
You must settle whether the two lanes share rate-limit state (the token bucket keyed per user×channel) — if shared, a user flooding OTPs can drain the very bucket urgent traffic depends on.

Even with lanes split, the low tier still needs protection from starvation: if urgent never lets up, marketing can wait indefinitely — the fix is aging (raising priority of jobs past an age threshold) or guaranteeing the low tier a minimum worker pool/quota.
Do not log-and-swallow the error — that would lose the email with nothing to show for it.
Each channel keeps a provider chain of [primary, fallback], and the dispatcher tries the primary first.
The moment the primary throws, the dispatcher immediately tries the fallback within that same processing attempt — milliseconds, not waiting for the queue's backoff.
The email still goes out, just through the fallback tier.
Provider chains are per-channel and independent, so email failing over to its fallback doesn't touch sms — sms keeps sending through its own primary the entire time.
Only if BOTH the email primary and the email fallback fail does the error get allowed to escape up to the job level.
The queue then retries the whole job per its attempts + backoff, giving the flapping provider time to recover.
Once those attempts run out, the job lands in the dead-letter/failed set for an operator to dig into — rather than being retried forever or dropped silently.
The request becomes three separate jobs — push, email, sms — each an independent unit built by the fan-out step and enqueued together.
Push and sms deliver on attempt 1 and are acked (the processor returns normally, so the job is removed from the queue for good).
The email job throws on attempt 1.
The broker records that failed attempt and requeues the same job per the exponential backoff, spacing out the retry so the flapping provider has time to recover.
On attempt 2 the email job succeeds and is acked.
The email retry touches only the email job — push and sms were already acked before email even gets its second attempt, so they are completely untouched.

Had all three channels been bundled into one job instead, the email failure would force the broker to retry the entire job, re-running push and sms too and producing duplicate sends for channels that had already succeeded.
That independence — one job per channel, each with its own retry and its own ack — is exactly why fan-out is built this way instead of one job per request.

Sorting at the producer only holds order within one batch — once an OTP arrives after marketing is already sitting in the queue, a producer-side sort has no way left to reorder what's already enqueued.
Priority has to live inside the queue itself, as a numeric attribute on each job.
The broker always hands the lowest-numbered (most urgent) waiting job to the next free worker, so the late OTP overtakes right at the next dequeue.
The worker needs no priority logic whatsoever — it just processes whatever job the broker hands it, which is already the highest-priority job waiting.
Priority is just a label-to-number mapping rather than hardcoded if/else branching, so adding a third tier is cheap.
Inserting transactional = 5 between otp = 1 and marketing = 10 is a one-line change to that mapping.
Nothing about the queue mechanism itself has to change to support the new tier — the broker still dequeues by lowest number and the worker still needs zero priority-aware code.
